Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP View image in fullscreen Virgin and Qantas planes at Sydney airport. A runway incursion on Sunday is being investigated by the transport safety bureau. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Transport Sydney airport incident involving Virgin and Qantas flights didn’t have to be reported, Airservices Australia says Airservices boss says planes remained 1km apart so runway incursion ‘didn’t meet mandatory reporting requirements’ but safety bureau is ‘concerned’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jonathan Barrett Business editor Thu 13 Aug 2026 23.32 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 01.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The organisation that manages Australian skies has defended its decision not to immediately report a fresh safety incident at Sydney airport when a Virgin plane aborted its takeoff. The chief executive of the commonwealth-owned Airservices Australia, Rob Sharp, said he did not believe the incident met the reporting threshold, given the substantial distance between the Virgin plane and a Qantas aircraft crossing the runway in front of it on Sunday. Sharp said air traffic controllers rescinded clearances while the aircraft were still more than 1km apart. Transport watchdog investigates third near-miss at Sydney airport Read more “Based on that criteria, it didn’t meet the mandatory reporting requirements from our perspective,” Sharp said on Friday. “However, we’re quite open to reviewing the data that surrounds it. If there are improvements to be made, we will make them.” The incident was referred to the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) on Thursday – four days after the event. It was the third safety issue at the country’s busiest airport in recent weeks. There are about 60 “runway incursions” a year in Australia, according to the ATSB, but they rarely happen at major airports or with large aircraft. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The pilot of the Virgin flight saw the Qantas plane transiting in front of it , reduced thrust and brought the aircraft to a stop at about the same time the clearance was rescinded. Sunday’s incident took place just a few hours after a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided colliding with a Qatar Airways plane on the Sydney tarmac, prompting nationwide attention on a shortage of air traffic controllers . A third incident occurred in late July, when a Qantas flight was initially cleared to cross a runway in front of another plane that had just landed. The three incidents are under investigation. The ATSB chief commissioner, Angus Mitchell, said he was seeking reasons for the delayed report of the latest incident. “This type of runway incursion and loss of separation is a transport safety concern, and we immediately commenced an investigation upon being notified of this yesterday afternoon,” Mitchell said on Friday. The safety bureau boss said while it was “too early to make any conclusions”, the ATSB would “consider any organisational or systemic issues that may have contributed” to the incident involving the Virgin and Qantas planes. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion ‘Training situation’ The ATSB disclosed there was a “supervisory or training situation” at the Sydney control tower at the time. Airservices said the controller who issued the initial takeoff clearance was an experienced worker undertaking an “endorsement check”. The worker was being monitored by another experienced controller, who promptly ordered that the clearance be cancelled. Endorsements refer to the qualification process required for a controller to hold different roles, such as overseeing taxiways and runways. Current staffing shortages are linked to a pandemic redundancy program whereby 140 experienced controllers left, according to the air traffic controllers’ union, Civil Air. Newer staff have fewer endorsements, which makes it difficult to plug holes in rosters and can lead to flight delays. The Civil Air president, Scott Nugent, said controllers “increase the spacing between aircraft” to maintain safety when there were fewer staff. On Saturday, before Sunday’s two incidents, more than 150 flights passing through Sydney were delayed due to a lack of air traffic controllers. Newsflash Newsroom , 30.08.2026, 13:49 Politics. President Nicușor Dan and parliamentary parties will hold fresh talks on September 1 to designate the next Prime Minister. The president believes that a majority for a stable government will be found this time. He explained that he did not make any further nominations in recent months because the successive failure of rejecting prime ministerial proposals would have harmed Romania’s economic image. This time, the president ruled out the option of a technocratic team, saying that the future cabinet will be composed mainly of ministers designated by the parliamentary parties. According to political sources, the future prime minister may be an independent leading a majority Social-Democratic government that will also be supported in Parliament by the Democratic Union of Ethnic Hungarians in Romania. EU funding. Romania is to finalise major projects funded under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan on the very last day of the deadline for the implementation of the plan. The opening of a new 47-km section of the A7 motorway, linking the capital Bucharest and the city of Bacău in the northeast, is scheduled for August 31. Horațiu Cosma, State Secretary at the Ministry of Transport, said in an online post that this milestone secures a 1.5 billion euro tranche of non-repayable funding. He further noted that future efforts would focus on the section between Bacău and the town of Pașcani, some 80 kilometers north of Bacău. The goal is to finalise 320 km of this motorway, which goes from Ploiești (in the south) to Pașcani, by early next year. Known as the Moldova Motorway or the “motorway of the Union of the Romanian Principalities,” the route will eventually cover over 450 km, connecting Bucharest to the northern border with Ukraine. Diesel. The Romanian finance ministry will cut the excise duty on diesel by another 5%, following an initial 20% reduction decided two weeks ago under a special law passed this year. The measure, which will apply from September 1 to 15, follows a new bi-weekly assessment and was adopted against the backdrop of rising crude oil prices on international markets. The ministry says the additional cut in excise duties on diesel aims to limit the ripple effect of fuel costs, particularly in the transport sector, which directly impacts consumer goods prices. According to the Price Monitor app, a liter of standard diesel in Bucharest was approximately 10.15 lei (some 1.93 euros) on Sunday morning. Danube. The Danube’s flow rate on entry to Romania is still below the multi-year average. Hydrologists say the slight increase seen in recent days will slow down, and the river’s flow will once again decline to reach 1,500 cubic meters per second. For several weeks, the flow rate was well below the average for this period, which is at 3,800–3,900 cubic meters per second. Due to low water levels, the two reactors at the Cernavodă nuclear power plant have been shut down, resulting in a 20% reduction in national electricity output. Consequently, during periods of peak domestic demand, Romania is importing large quantities of electricity from neighbouring countries, often at prices two to three times higher than export rates. EU. European Council President António Costa is touring the capitals of EU member states until September 17. He aims to identify the specific priorities and concerns of each country as the summer recess ends and European institutions resume work next week. Costa is scheduled to visit Bucharest, Sofia, and Athens on September 3. Talks with the leaders of member states will focus defense, competitiveness, EU enlargement, support for Ukraine, and the Union’s future multiannual budget for the 2028–2034 period, among others. According to the international media, Costa is seeking support for the introduction of new levies to bolster European finances. Under a proposal made last year by the European Commission, the future multiannual budget is set to reach 2 trillion euros, the largest in the history of the EU’s common fund. The European Council President has already visited Slovakia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and the Czech Republic. Nepal. More than 650 tourists are reported missing in Nepal, out of a total of nearly 2,500 people identified so far as missing following the catastrophic floods five days ago. According to the National Tourism Board, cited by Agence France-Presse, the majority are Nepalese, followed by Chinese, Indian, American, and Ukrainian nationals. Citizens from 31 other countries are also among the missing. Nepalese authorities have not yet provided an exact figure of the fatalities among foreign nationals due to identification difficulties. For its part, China has reported approximately 260 foreign nationals among the more than 540 missing persons. According to the Foreign Ministry in Bucharest, there is currently no information as to whether Romanian citizens were affected by the disaster in Nepal. https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: More than 52,000 recalls to prison were recorded in England and Wales in the year to June, a rise of 27% on the previous 12 months. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA View image in fullscreen More than 52,000 recalls to prison were recorded in England and Wales in the year to June, a rise of 27% on the previous 12 months. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA Prisons and probation More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales Ministry of Justice figures show recalls rose 27% in year to June despite emergency measures to ease overcrowding Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 14.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday. Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released. A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total. The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month. The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis. The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said. The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026. The Howard League for Penal Reform said the “alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse”, as it called on the government to find a “lasting solution” to the overcrowding crisis. Rob Preece, the head of communications at the Howard League, said: “The prison system is under enormous pressure, with chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and awful conditions that make it close to impossible to rehabilitate people effectively. Imposing ever longer sentences has led us to this crisis, but the alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse.” The MoJ said it was “vital those who break the rules can be hauled back to prison”. The department said the rise in recalls amid SDS40 releases was also likely to have been influenced by policy changes that result in most offenders being taken back into custody for 56 days before being released again – known as a fixed-term recall – instead of being held until the end of their sentence. Incidents of self-harm and violence have remained high as pressure on the prison system has grown. Safety in custody statistics showed that 360 people in prison died in the 12 months to the end of September 2026, including 66 people who died in circumstances recorded as “self-inflicted”. Prisons recorded 68,231 incidents of self-harm in the 12 months to the end of June 2026, at a rate of one every eight minutes. Self-harm incidents fell by 12% in men’s prisons and fell by 3.8% in women’s prisons. A separate dataset showed that the number of serious offenders on probation who were charged with a serious further offence increased for the third successive year to a record number. Of 281 serious offenders charged, 119 were registered sexual offenders, 128 were murderers, and four were terrorists or posed a terror risk, according to figures on multi-agency public protection arrangements. https://www.politico.eu/article/ursula-v.text: MONTREAL, Canada — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday she aims to bring EU-Canada relations to the “highest level possible,” touting potential associate member status in the bloc for Ottawa despite capitals having rejected the term a day earlier. Von der Leyen’s overture comes on the eve of a landmark EU-Canada summit in Montreal where she and Prime Minister Mark Carney are due to announce plans for deeper cooperation against a backdrop of rising autocracy globally and unpredictable relations with U.S. President Donald Trump. “Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said in a speech hosted by the C.D. Howe Institute. “This is why we are discussing the idea of Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union.” Advertisement Advertisement No sooner had von der Leyen finished speaking than German Chancellor Friedrich Merz issued a statement saying that the EU and Canada were establishing an “Alliance for the Future” — without mentioning the associate member status. Germany has led the opposition to using the term, according to EU diplomats. “We are fighting each other about a few words which von der Leyen pulled out of thin air,” one of those EU diplomats told POLITICO on Wednesday. “It’s a bit silly while we should have ambition and focus on other things. This is not our proudest moment.” In a speech hours later on the sidelines of the summit, European Council President António Costa sought to bridge the divide by playing down the importance of the term. “Tomorrow, the European Union and Canada will launch an Alliance for the Future of Europe,” he said in a nod to Merz’s statement and using the term preferred by Carney to describe the relationship. “President von der Leyen has even put forward the bold idea of making Canada an ‘associate member’ of the European Union,” he said, noting “I share her ambition.” “Whether that ends up being the term or not, one thing is clear: our partnership will be the closest, deepest and most unique of its kind,” he added. Advertisement Advertisement The Commission president said in her speech that talks about associate membership would focus on deeper cooperation across AI, climate and energy policy, as well as bolstering shared work between the European Commission and the Canadian government as well as “Parliament to Parliament” and “Court to Court,” a reference to the European Court of Justice and Canada’s Supreme Court. Such a status, she said, would be open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe, who are ready to open a new frontier together — and to chart the course together, to think beyond the terms of our partnership today, toward the most ambitious vision we can build.” Von der Leyen’s use of the term associate membership — which she first mentioned in September — is likely to rub some EU capitals the wrong way after a group of countries led by Germany objected to including a reference to the term in a joint EU-Canada statement that was seen by POLITICO and is due to be published on Friday. After days of talks, EU countries opted for softer language to describe the two sides’ future relations, including the “Alliance for the Future” — the term used by the Canadian side — as well as an “even closer association ... short of full membership.” EU diplomats have told POLITICO that while capitals support the broader aim of closer ties with Canada, they are wary of offering a status that has never been proposed before and whose legal contours remain undefined. Berlin had previously floated associate member status for Ukraine, including specific privileges such as observer status in the European Commission, but that effort was rejected. Reacting to reports that EU countries would drop the “associate member” term, Carney said on Tuesday: “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians … and Canada as a whole becoming a more independent, more sovereign nation, so we can live our lives as we choose.” Advertisement Advertisement Both Carney and von der Leyen have cast this week’s summit as part of a broader effort to deepen ties at a time when both Ottawa and Brussels have clashed with the Trump administration, with von der Leyen warning in her speech about “deeper decay in the international order.” “Alliances and assumptions that have enabled our prosperity and security are changing rapidly, and each nation or region is looking at how to secure its own interests and its own independence,” she said. “We can no longer let ourselves be shackled by the limits of the old-world order.” This story has been updated. Camille Gijs contributed reporting from Brussels.
